Here are a couple of examples of using and responding to AI in this project.

## Example 1

### Background

My initial thought of how to measure normality was to cacluate the mean squared error of the Q-Q plot. AI informed me that R\^2 would be a better fit for accomplishing roughly the same thing (namely, that the shape roughly fits). After it explained how R\^2 worked, I asked the following:

### The prompt

I could expect this method to throw a false positive of R is close to -1 instead of 1, but that would require the data to be perfectly negatively correlated with the expected. Is there any scenario in which that would happen?

### Explanation

This demonstrates both reading and understanding the examples and trying to come up with a situation in which this method may not work, since it was not one I was familiar with. I also try to phrase questions in such a way that finding a disagreement or contradiction if I want to ensure there isn't one involves answering the question affirmatively.

## Example 2

### Background

This example is not an example of me responding critically, but instead on example of giving very detailed instructions rather than vague instructions that are up to interpretation.

### The prompt

I've uploaded a source titled "initial_simulation_template.md". It's a compilation of the code for the graphs you've given me, with some tweaks. Notably:

1.  The naming scheme has changed. The histogram and Q-Q plot at the end are now called "v1" and "v2" (v for visual.) I'm resetting the numbering scheme here because other distributions may require more than three plots in order to narrow down on the exact lowest n that meets all three requirements (for example, I'd generate some graphs of skewness with high n for the exponential distribution.) However, the visual graphs will always only need to be generated exactly once.

2.  The visual graphs are pulling directly from the initially generated results. The code for this section initially called the variable containing the initial results sim_data, but in the original code that creates the data, it's called results. This needs to match.

3.  The excess kurtosis and skewness graphs are now graphing the absolute value, and have their y axis minimums set to zero. The former is extremely important to match what I say I'm measuring; the latter is for visual neatness.

This is the format I'd like to use for all further distributions. When I say to run the initial simulation for a new type of distribution, use this format, changing the code for the distribution type as needed.

### Explanation

I initially tried sending the updated code as part of this prompt instead of as a file, but it turns out that Gemini has a character limit for its prompts. No matter how I ended up giving it this information, this prompt shows both that I send extremely detailed prompts and also that I change the code generated by AI if it's not behaving quite the way that I need.
